description:
Ship v1.0 of just-in-time as a tagged, installable release, and close the documentation-tooling and repository-quality defects that remain in the milestone.

## Background

The product surfaces — native CLI, Rust server and API, built web UI, and MCP server — are mature and covered by tests, but the repository has never been tagged. The release path is still the packaging-only workflow that predates the current component set: it does not run the security audits, does not smoke-test what it packages, and publishes no versioned artifact that an adopter can install.

Three conditions shape the release contract. Dependency audits are advisory rather than blocking, so a known advisory can reach a tag. The container story exposes four overlapping image definitions, one of which runs nginx, Node, and a background-process supervisor as root. Installation and deployment facts are repeated across the README, the installation guide, the deployment how-to, and the MCP component README, so each correction has to be applied several times or drifts.

v1.0 publishes one channel: a GitHub release carrying Linux x86_64 musl binaries and the packed MCP tarball. Registry publication for npm and for container images is deliberately out of scope, so the release requires no stored publishing credential and no registry account. Distribution breadth is a later decision, taken once the release path itself is proven.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The supported v1.0 capability set is the native CLI, the Rust server and API, the built web UI, and the MCP server. Removals are limited to redundant packaging, redundant deployment topologies, and repeated prose; no product capability is withdrawn.
- [hard] REQ-02: `cargo audit`, `npm audit --omit=dev` in `web/`, and `npm audit --omit=dev` in `mcp-server/` report no advisories against the committed locks at the tagged commit. Dependencies without a safe upgrade are removed or replaced, and no advisory allowlist or ignore list is introduced.
- [hard] REQ-03: The security workflow runs on pull requests and through `workflow_call`, fails on audit-tool installation errors as well as on findings, contains no `continue-on-error` or shell fallback, and is a required predecessor of every artifact-producing job in the release workflow.
- [hard] REQ-04: Every committed workflow validates under a pinned `actionlint`, and every external action or reusable-workflow reference on the CI, security, container, and release paths is a full 40-character commit SHA carrying a human-readable version comment. A documented update procedure records the upstream release, changelog, and permission delta for each pin change.
- [hard] REQ-05: Workspace `rust-version` is 1.97, every crate inherits that single declaration, and CI builds and tests the workspace with exactly that compiler. One documented policy states how the declaration is refreshed when it falls more than one stable release behind, without copying the current stable version into workflow configuration or prose.
- [hard] REQ-06: One production image serves the API and the built web UI from a single non-root `jit-server` running as PID 1, against a whole repository bind-mounted at `/repo`, with a health check and a bounded signal shutdown that exits cleanly. The CLI image, the split API and web images, and the previous all-in-one image no longer exist; the Compose example runs the one supported service; and every active script, fixture, and document uses that contract. Pull requests build and runtime-smoke the image, and no job publishes it to a registry.
- [hard] REQ-07: `jit`, `jit-server`, the MCP package, and the web package each declare `1.0.0`, and a check rejects a release tag, manifest, or documented compatibility version that disagrees with the others. The product version stays distinguishable from the `.jit` repository format version.
- [hard] REQ-08: README, installation, deployment, MCP, and component documentation each serve a distinct audience purpose and link to a canonical page instead of repeating commands, support matrices, configuration facts, or guarantees. Every removed walkthrough leaves a context-bearing link from its former entry point, and the result passes mechanical and adversarial documentation review.
- [hard] REQ-09: Pushing an annotated `v1.0.0` tag runs one workflow that executes the normal validation suites and the blocking audits on the tagged commit, builds the Linux x86_64 musl `jit` and `jit-server` archive and the packed MCP tarball, smoke-tests the extracted binaries before any publication step, and publishes one GitHub release carrying those artifacts, their SHA-256 checksums, both license texts, and release notes describing supported capabilities and upgrade expectations.
- [hard] REQ-10: The `v1.0.0` GitHub release is the only channel v1.0 publishes. No npm registry version, no container registry tag, and no separately produced source distribution is published or claimed, and the installation, deployment, and MCP documentation describe the supported paths on that basis.
- [hard] REQ-11: The documentation-tooling and repository-quality defects consumed by this container reach `Done` before the release tag is created, and the tagged commit passes repository validation with no reported drift.

## Notes

Supersedes the rejected production-readiness epic, whose release design specified a crash-recoverable multi-workflow publication protocol — immutable candidate escrow, transition ledgers, a fixed-ref tag authority, and reconstruction from expired evidence. That protocol defended against failures whose recovery cost, for an unreleased project with no downstream consumers, is deleting a tag and cutting another one. The work that survives is the product and repository hardening it wrapped: advisory remediation, blocking audits, action pinning, the consolidated image, version alignment, MSRV enforcement, and documentation canonicalization.

Release authority is the maintainer pushing an annotated tag. The workflow reacts to that tag; it never creates one.
title: Version 1.0 release
